articles.title: Nordio sugli stipendi dei magistrati dopo il no di Meloni: "Le sentenze vanno attuate". Il...
articles.summary: AGI - "Ho applaudito alla fine, anche nell'intermezzo qualche volta, non sempre, ma qualche volta, quando ha detto che dobbiamo lavorare insieme, perché questo è". Lo dice il ministro della Giustizia, Carlo Nordio , intervenendo al 37esimo congresso dell'Anm in corso a Napoli. "La perpetuità del conflitto che c'è stato nei tempi del referendum è stata superata - sottolinea - ora l'inverno, non dico del nostro scontento, ma l'inverno del nostro dissidio si è composto, si sta ricomponendo in un momento in cui occorre riflettere su ciò che possiamo fare insieme e le cose che possiamo e dobbiamo fare insieme sono molte". "Il principio è l'atmosfera in cui si svolge questo incontro, per il quale vi ringrazio anche per l'accoglienza e per l'invito che mi è stato fatto", aggiunge. Nordio: "Le sentenze vanno eseguite, i magistrati accettino di rateizzare gli stipendi" "Le sentenze vanno eseguite. E quindi una sentenza del Consiglio di Stato definitiva va attuata. Io confido molto nella sensibilità della stessa magistratura associata affinché vi sia non certo una rinuncia a quello che è un diritto acquisito secondo una sentenza, ma nella attuazione di questa sentenza, che, visto il momento di grave sacrificio un po' per tutti in Italia, può e deve essere, secondo me, proprio in ragione di opportunità e di sensibilità, essere magari differito o rateizzato o spalmato", ha risposto Nordio ai giornalisti sulla questione degli stipendi arretrati dei magistrati. La precisazione del ministero: nessun contrasto Nordio-Meloni Nordio si dice "sorpreso, per non dire sbigottito" , di fronte a "un nuovo tentativo di strumentalizzazione delle sue parole che, questa volta, lo vorrebbe in contrasto con la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni". È quanto fa sapere via Arenula in una nota, sottolineando che, in merito alla dichiarazione a margine del 37esimo congresso dell'Anm, il Guardasigilli, interpellato sulla vicenda della recente pronuncia del Consiglio di Stato sugli arretrati dei magistrati, "ha invece sostenuto la posizione della premier". In un "momento di profonda crisi per tutti", e "pur nella consapevolezza che le sentenze vadano rispettate", il ministro, si legge ancora nella nota, ha "semplicemente auspicato da parte dei magistrati una mozione dei sentimenti per trovare una soluzione comune". articles.body:
Italy and Kuwait say an Iranian drone was involved, but Tehran says the US and Israel may be looking to escalate the war.

Tehran, Iran – The deaths of two Italians in Kuwait in an alleged Iranian attack could worsen relations between Iran and the European Union, warn experts.

Antonio Saccoccio, 65, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, were working for a European defence company in Kuwait when they were killed in a drone attack on a military site on Thursday.

Iran has officially denied any role in their deaths, calling it a “false flag” operation intended to draw European countries, which have not officially joined the United States and Israel in strikes on Iran, deeper into the conflict.

Riccardo Alcaro, research coordinator and head of the global competition and political risk programme at the Rome-based Istituto Affari Internazionali (IAI), said the reasons why Iran might deny any responsibility for the attack remain unclear.

“Assuming that the drone was launched by an Iraqi pro-Iranian group, the intention would be to degrade Kuwait’s defence capabilities ahead of a possible new confrontation with the US, which Tehran considers very much possible if not likely and hopes it can deter through such actions,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Their insistence on denying responsibility would reflect a dual objective: avoiding being seen as the aggressor while reinforcing the false flag operation narrative, thereby making it easier to challenge the rationale for a possible future US-Israeli attack.”

Divisions

Politically, the deaths could become a sensitive issue in Europe if public opinion starts associating such incidents with the unpopular war launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, crippling energy supplies and driving up prices of gas and petrol worldwide.

Alcaro believes the response from Italy and Europe will be to continue condemning attacks against countries in the region. Countries whose companies operate as contractors at military bases in Kuwait, which has suffered a series of Iranian attacks in recent weeks, will also have to review security protocols for personnel working at sensitive sites, he added.

“Weapon systems, such as the radar that the two Italian nationals were servicing, are highly complex and require continuous technical support, which can probably only be provided by specialised personnel as the case with the Italian Rheinmetall workers shows. This exposes their personnel to these kinds of risks,” he said.

A second narrative coming from state-aligned circles and media in Tehran specifically implicates Ukraine and redirects attention towards Europe’s role in the war – even as Italy and Kuwait accuse Iran.

The deaths follow an attack by Ukraine on two Russian vessels in Libya on Sunday, prompting widespread anger at Kyiv for appearing to drag its war with Moscow into the Middle East theatre.

Foad Izadi, another Tehran-based conservative political commentator, told Al Jazeera that he believes Ukraine was the culprit in a false flag operation.

Izadi, who is an associate professor at the faculty of world studies at the University of Tehran, said European leaders had “the blood of the Iranian people on their hands” for playing a supporting role for US aircraft and operations.

He pointed to statements made by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte that confirmed up to 5,000 US military sorties originated from European bases in support of Operation Epic Fury between February 28 and mid-April.

Approximately 500 US military flights had taken off from bases in Italy in support of the operation, Rutte said in late June. Italy’s Defence Ministry insisted that it had authorised only routine logistical and technical operations, not combat missions.

Relations between Iran and the EU have nosedived in recent years over a range of issues, including Iran’s contentious nuclear programme and regional influence. The bloc has imposed many sanctions on Iran and considers the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a major faction in the Iranian political and military establishment, a “terrorist” organisation.

Izadi said he does not expect relations to improve over the coming years, but said the lingering conflict would only hurt European consumers who are now contending with considerably higher gas and other energy prices for winter.

“It is not to Europe’s benefit to be entangled in prolonged energy wars with Russia or Iran,” he said.

Official response

Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said military installations were targeted in Kuwait and that the deaths of “technicians” maintaining detection antennae for a Skyguard air defence system were caused by intercepted drone shrapnel.

The official response from Iranian authorities has shifted between blame on other actors and denial. Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs was quick to reject responsibility.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war,” wrote Iran’s chief diplomat Abbas Araghchi on X, adding that he called his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts to offer condolences.

Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, Iran’s armed forces spokesman, also issued a stern rejection and said the US and Israel have a history of launching false flag operations to advance their objectives involving Iran. He described the latest accusations against Iran as “a cover for maintaining hostilities and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region”.

State-linked media in Iran also largely reproduced official narratives, including claims of a nefarious covert operation by outside actors.

“False flag during situation of no war, no peace,” wrote the reformist Mardom Salari (rule of the people) newspaper, framing the Kuwait incident within the current precarious status quo.

But some also warned hardline factions in Tehran about the risk of such incidents escalating into all-out war. The state-linked Jomhouri-e Eslami (Islamic Republic) newspaper claimed that the US and Israeli spy agencies were looking for an “excuse” to restart large-scale combat operations against Iran, so Tehran should refrain from launching any preemptive strikes.

“Kuwait’s incident on Thursday showed that the theoreticians who speak and write of the necessity of Iran launching a preemptive attack are playing in the enemy’s court,” the outlet said in an editorial on Saturday, the first day of the week in Iran.

Rome has attributed the attack to Iranian-origin drones, but Foreign Minister Tajani acknowledged the possibility that Iran-aligned militias in other countries could have launched the projectiles. The Italian government has not yet vowed military retaliation, additional sanctions or other punitive measures against Iran.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc “must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks” on Kuwait and other regional Arab allies of the EU in order to ensure security for all.

James Moran, an associate senior fellow at the Brussels-based Centre for European Policy Studies, said he believes Iran’s denials lack credibility. The former EU diplomat told Al Jazeera that von der Leyen’s call for pressure likely means tightening EU sanctions on the Islamic Republic.

He said the Kuwait attack “will certainly have negative effects on EU-Iranian relations, but nobody expects the EU or Italy itself to get involved in any kinetic response”.

“The overriding EU position is against the US-Israeli war, which Europe considers illegal and counterproductive, not least because of the fallout for EU energy supplies, which are now costing Europe dear,” Moran said.

Investigations were opened in only 22.7 percent and indictments were filed in less than one percent of cases. The rise in army and settler attacks against Palestinians overlaps with the appointment of another settler to a top Israeli security position, as since July 2024, Avi Bluth, a settler, has been heading the military's West Bank command. Since his appointment, Bluth has led an extremely violent approach towards Palestinians, which includes razing entire refugee camps and relaxing the army's open-fire policy, while also advancing the establishment of settlements in the area. According to Ynet's report, most Jewish nationalist crimes in 2026 took place in areas north of Jerusalem, with the Nablus Governorate suffering more than 34 percent of the crimes recorded by the army. The governorate is the heart of a settlement resurgence in the area, as the Israeli far-right government, in the past four years, led a campaign to seize Palestinian land and establish settlements in the area. Other parts north of Jerusalem, such as the governorates of Ramallah, Tulkarm and Jenin, suffered together more than 33 percent of this year's crimes, while the area around East Jerusalem and the West Bank's southern parts of the territory, which include the governorates of Bethlehem and Hebron, suffered 30 percent of the attacks. The rest of the Jewish nationalist crimes were committed in the eastern part of the territory, in the Jordan Valley, where the Israeli army and the settlers expelled Palestinian communities from their land over the past years. articles.body:
Le parole di Ignazio La Russa, secondo cui un'eventuale bocciatura della nuova legge elettorale da parte della Consulta sarebbe "una violazione costituzionale e un aiuto alla sinistra", accendono lo scontro politico. Dura la reazione delle opposizioni con Elly Schlein in primis che parla di un'intimidazione nei confronti della Corte Costituzionale.

"È proprio inaccettabile l'intimidazione del presidente del Senato Ignazio La Russa alla Corte Costituzionale. Non è accettabile", ha detto la segretaria del Pd Elly Schlein intervenendo all'assemblea dei sindaci Dem a Verona. "Piantatela con gli attacchi alla magistratura e alle regole fondamentali del bilanciamento dei poteri tra lo Stato, avete già provato una volta a stravolgere la Costituzione e vi hanno fermato 15 milioni di persone".

"Il presidente La Russa ha confessato che hanno fatto la legge elettorale per colpire la sinistra - ha detto il il leader M5s, Giuseppe Conte -, per colpire il campo progressista e favorire la loro autoperpetuazione sulle poltrone. Il presidente del Senato, che è un'alta carica dello Stato, non può permettersi di esplicitare un'ingerenza così indebita nelle funzioni di competenza, nelle prerogative della Corte Costituzionale. Siamo in un'Italia democratica, con un assetto costituzionale che va rispettato".

articles.title: Bootleg alcohol poisonings in Iran see dozens dead and badly injured
articles.summary: A spate of alcohol poisonings in Iran has led to deaths and serious injuries including blindness.
articles.preview: A spate of alcohol poisonings in Iran has led to deaths and serious injuries including blindness. Two years after four people were executed for distributing contaminated alcoholic beverages – causing the deaths of 17 people and leaving 199 with injuries, including blindness – another spate of mass alcohol poisoning has swept through Iran.
articles.body:
A spate of alcohol poisonings in Iran has led to deaths and serious injuries including blindness.

Two years after four people were executed for distributing contaminated alcoholic beverages – causing the deaths of 17 people and leaving 199 with injuries, including blindness – another spate of mass alcohol poisoning has swept through Iran.

Since mid-November, more than 20 people have died and at least 500 have been poisoned from consuming methanol-contaminated alcohol, the same substance used in medical disinfectants and wound care, and potentially fatal if consumed.

The first death was reported on November 16 in Marvdasht, in Fars Province, central Iran. By Friday, 66 people in Fars Province, 126 in Hormozgan Province in southern Iran, 230 in Razavi Khorasan Province and 15 in West Azerbaijan Province had been poisoned.

Police have launched a crackdown on bootleg alcohol sellers since then and by Friday, about 10 people were arrested across Iran in connection with the cases.

On Friday, the prosecutor of Razavi Khorasan Province said that the poisoning cases in Razavi Khorasan, Fars and Hormozgan provinces were connected. But several individuals had been arrested in connection with a “contaminated alcohol distribution network”.

Banned

A former Tehran police detective, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that any investigation into these incidents will have to look at the wider bootleg alcohol industry to avoid repeat poisoning incidents.

“In cases such as methanol poisoning affecting several cities or provinces, investigators need to look beyond the distribution network and examine the production network as well,” he said.

“Sometimes distributors may not even know that the alcohol they are selling to the public is contaminated. In such cases, investigations usually continue until those responsible for producing the contaminated drinks are identified and apprehended.”

Laws in effect banning alcohol were established in 1980, shortly after the Islamic Revolution, although religious minorities such as Christians and Jews can still access beverages such as wine.

The sale and purchase of alcohol is illegal in Iran, with drinkers potentially facing punishments of 80 lashes and jail, while repeat offenders have been executed.

Despite the strict laws, Hossein Kermanpour, spokesperson for Iran’s Ministry of Health, recently repeated the government’s advice that people should avoid consuming alcohol – but if they do and experience unusual symptoms, they should seek immediate medical attention.

The use of cheap medical-grade alcohol as the base of their products has made the consumption of illicit alcoholic beverages highly risky, the former police detective said.

“They typically buy medical-grade ethanol and mix it with a certain percentage of grape or date-based alcohol before selling it. Some use tea or acorn extracts to alter the colour and taste, while others add tequila or whisky-like flavourings to imitate the taste and appearance of commercial spirits,” he said.

“The problem is that medical alcohol, which is supposed to be ethanol, can sometimes contain traces or higher concentrations of methanol due to various factors. If the ethanol used in production is contaminated with methanol, the resulting product can become extremely toxic. In such cases, even the producers themselves may be unaware that the alcohol they purchased was contaminated, potentially exposing consumers to serious poisoning.”

Medical issues

Iranians say that alcohol is said to be available in major cities, and two official studies conducted in the early 2010s found an increase in alcohol consumption among Iranians aged between 15 and 64.

The National Mental Health Survey commissioned by the Ministry of Health in 2011 estimated that 830 per 100,000 people (approximately 623,000 individuals) had alcohol dependence, while 2,800 per 100,000 were recreational drinkers. A second survey also reported that there was a particular increase in alcohol consumption among people aged under 18 and women. A more recent study by the Ministry of Health in 2021 gave a more mixed assessment about any rise in alcohol use in Iran.

Dr Shadi Hassanzadeh, a general practitioner in Mashhad, told Al Jazeera that only when patients experience extreme medical issues – such as blurred vision, progressive loss of consciousness, and seizures – do they realise this is not ordinary intoxication and seek help, although by then it might be too late to save their eyesight.

“Methanol, or industrial alcohol, is extremely dangerous when used in homemade alcoholic drinks because consumers have no way of detecting its presence. By the time its effects become apparent, serious damage may already have been done to the body,” said Hassanzadeh.

Maryam, a nurse at an ophthalmology hospital in Tehran, told Al Jazeera that despite the law, she does not see people admitted with alcohol-related incidents afraid to reveal consumption of illicit alcohol.

“Since there is a widespread belief that consuming industrial alcohol causes blindness, ophthalmology hospitals are among the first places people turn to for treatment. The most common symptoms they present with are vision problems,” she said.

“Most people do not realise that seeking medical attention soon after consuming industrial alcohol increases their chances of saving their eyesight. Because they often do not know they have been poisoned, they delay seeking treatment until it is too late for doctors to do anything.”

Most cases of alcohol poisoning happen during weekends and national celebrations, she said, when Iranians have a respite from gruelling work and education schedules.

“During the first 24 hours after consuming methanol, the symptoms can resemble those of an ordinary hangover, making it difficult for people to recognise the danger,” she said. “They may only realise something is seriously wrong around 72 hours after consumption, when the symptoms become more severe,” she said.

articles.body:
Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said.

MSF said Israel had directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.

The head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned the bombing, saying: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”

In a post on X, Ghebreyesus also said: “Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable … These attacks MUST STOP.”

The Israeli military claimed that the two men whom they killed, Ahmad Abou Hassira and Moaz Alitsbach, were members of Hamas’s military wing. It also added that the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and had caused no damage to the facility.

The Israeli military has often accused Hamas of embedding itself within civilian infrastructure, including hospitals. However, in 2024 the head of the international criminal court’s Palestine investigation said claims about the presence of Hamas fighters in Gaza’s hospitals had been “grossly exaggerated”.

Israel has killed Palestinian medical workers en masse since the start of the war in Gaza. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, at least 1,700 have been killed by Israeli attacks. Rights groups say the Israeli military has engaged in systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, including medical infrastructure.

The UN has repeatedly called on Israel to stop its restrictions on the entry of supplies to allow Palestinians to prepare for the winter and begin to rebuild the destroyed strip.

The result is a healthcare system “experiencing systemic collapse, severely undermining its capacity to meet the basic health needs of the civilian population”, according to a UN report in August.

The humanitarian situation is also deteriorating, as heavy rains exacerbate crowded and unsanitary living conditions, leading to the spread of infectious diseases.

Israel has continued to bomb Gaza on a near-daily basis despite a ceasefire signed in October 2025, killing at least 1,705 people since then. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of violating the understandings of the ceasefire.

The war began after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 that killed about 1,200 people.

More than 74,000 people have been killed and more than 175,000 injured in Israel’s war in Gaza. A UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes. Israel denies these claims.

articles.title: As Spain votes, what could change for Europe?
articles.summary: Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza.
articles.preview: Spain's election could bring change for Europe November 28, 2026 Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza. Walking through the halls of the European institutions in Brussels these days, it feels as if people are whispering about the end of an era. What happens when one of the most vocal leaders of Europe's center left is no longer at the table?
articles.body:
Spain's election could bring change for Europe

November 28, 2026

Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza.

Walking through the halls of the European institutions in Brussels these days, it feels as if people are whispering about the end of an era. What happens when one of the most vocal leaders of Europe's center left is no longer at the table?

Pedro Sanchez is one of the few social democratic prime ministers left in the European Union, and Spain is the largest member state still led by one. That's why this election raises questions that go beyond who governs in Madrid.

After more than eight years in office Sanchez called a snap election at the beginning of October, three days after parliament rejected two emergency decrees aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis. Anger over soaring housing costs has brought protesters onto the streets nationwide this year.

Sanchez's minority government was already under pressure over its handling of the summer migration crisis in Ceuta and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife have denied.

Polls on Monday predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) at around 32% and the Socialists led by Sanchez at 31%.

With the right-wing populist Vox party in third place at around 17%, the polling projected an absolute majority for the PP and Vox combined. The two parties would still have to decide whether they want to govern together.

Important center-left voice may be 'silenced'

A change of government in Madrid would cost Europe's center left one of its most influential voices, Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre in Brussels, told DW. "This voice might now be silenced."

Carbonell said three positions have set Sanchez apart: his willingness to challenge US President Donald Trump, his support for Palestinian statehood and his defense of immigration into Europe. Sanchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have continued to argue that migrant workers help fill labor shortages, support an aging Spanish and European population and sustain growth.

Earlier this year, his government opened a program to grant legal status to eligible migrants already living in Spain. It received more than 1 million applications. Spain's economy grew by 2.6% last year, nearly double the eurozone average, and the government expects GDP to grow by 2.6% this year and 2.2% in 2027.

Will Spain take a tougher line on migration?

The conservative PP has campaigned for tighter immigration controls while keeping routes open for workers in sectors facing shortages. Vox wants sharper cuts to immigration, more deportations and an end to regularization for new arrivals. It also wants Spanish citizens to get priority for subsidized housing and other social benefits.

This stance is nothing new at the European level. "With a PP-Vox government, Spain would join the general European trend towards an anti-immigration policy," said Carbonell, adding that he could see Madrid moving closer to countries pushing for tougher return policies. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are already in talks with Rwanda about setting up a hub for people whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Camino Mortera-Martinez, an associate fellow at the Centre for European Reform, agrees that a shift in Madrid would reinforce a trend already underway in Europe. "This anti-migration tendency doesn't come from European leaders, but from voters," she told DW.

PP, Vox back higher defense spending

Another domain where Spain could potentially change course and influence its European neighbors concerns its defense policies. Spain raised defense spending from 1.24% of GDP in 2024 to 2% in 2025, reaching NATO's previous benchmark.

Nevertheless, Sanchez has pushed back against the alliance's new annual target of 5% of GDP by 2035, which includes both military spending and broader security investments. He has argued that Spain could meet its NATO capability commitments by spending around 2.1% of GDP.

Both the PP and Vox favor higher defense investment but leave the exact figure open in their election programs. "They have a voting base that has no problem to increase defense spending, contrary to Sanchez," said Mortera-Martinez.

A shift on Israel and Palestinian statehood?

Mortera-Martinez also expects a change in Spain's approach to the Middle East, should Sanchez lose the election.

"The current government has been at the forefront of defending the last bastions of international and public law," she said.

Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sanchez has accused European leaders of applying double standards by rallying behind Ukraine against Russia's invasion, while failing to defend international law with the same resolve in the Middle East. In April, he pushed to suspend the EU's agreement with Israel, which makes respect for human rights an essential part of the relationship.

Carbonell, too, believes a new conservative government would be less vocal in its support for the Palestinians. "Sanchez was able to influence people on the subject matter, moving the consensus a bit more towards pro-Palestine," he said.

If Sanchez comes up short on Sunday, Europe's social democrats would lose their strongest foothold among the EU's largest countries. But, said Carbonell, a defeat in Spain could reignite a debate across the European center left about how to win back voters and stay politically relevant elsewhere.

articles.title: Kyiv embraces expansion of conflict beyond Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine has grown bolder in recent days, striking Russian ships in the Baltic Sea and the Mediterranean, as far afield as the Libyan port of Benghazi. Kyiv seeks to encourage the Western alliance to continue supporting the country. But faced with this latest escalation, European leaders are torn between supporting Ukraine and growing concerned.

Kyiv seeks to encourage the Western alliance to continue supporting the country. But faced with this latest escalation, European leaders are torn between supporting Ukraine and growing concerned.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky struck a paternalistic tone. "[Vladimir Putin] is an aggressor and a killer... He can't be a friend," he said in a soft voice during an interview with the BBC on Friday, November 27. It was as if he were reminding his ally Donald Trump of some basic ethical principles, 10 days after the White House occupant called the Russian president a "friend." "It's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said.

"It's like someone saying during World War II that Hitler was a good friend," Zelensky continued, emphasizing that Trump's missteps threaten to put the United States on the wrong side of history. The time when the Ukrainian leader made sure not to upset Trump is truly over. The Trump administration's "betrayal" – its willingness since October 9 to do business with Russia when it announced an agreement to supply Russian diesel – followed by the Republicans' defeat in November 3 midterm elections, seems to have given Zelensky newfound freedom to speak out.

articles.title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
articles.summary: The Israeli military says it targeted "Hamas terrorists" in the strike which has been condemned by the World Health Organization.
articles.preview: Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation. MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military. In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
articles.body:
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.

MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".

In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."

In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".

The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".

Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.

Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.

Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.

Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.

"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.

He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.

The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.

Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Meloni sente Zelensky: "No a iniziative che mettano a rischio la sicurezza dell'Italia"

Lo comunica Palazzo Chigi in una nota, in cui si spiega che la premier, nel ribadire il sostegno dell'Italia all'Ucraina nel percorso verso una pace giusta e duratura, ha precisato che questo sostegno non può tradursi nell'accettazione di iniziative che mettano a rischio la sicurezza dell'Italia e della regione . Meloni e Zelensky a colloquio: "Il raid in Libia non coordinato con i partner" Il presidente Zelensky ha confermato che l'operazione in Libia è stata condotta senza coordinamento preventivo con i partner . Ha assicurato di aver compreso le preoccupazioni italiane e si è impegnato a garantire una piena condivisione delle informazioni e una comunicazione diretta e costante, spiega la nota. "Abbiamo discusso delle questioni su cui stiamo lavorando. E' importante che ci comprendiamo ", ha scritto il presidente ucraino su X. "Ho anche affermato che ci impegniamo a garantire lo scambio di tutte le informazioni necessarie tra le autorità competenti dei nostri Paesi e a mantenere una comunicazione diretta, regolare ed efficace", ha spiegato ancora.

articles.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
articles.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
articles.preview: Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over. Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way.
articles.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% â way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method â sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia â "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a cafÃ© here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
articles.preview: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives. In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin. "Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

- Published20 November

- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published7 days ago

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
articles.summary: The ChatGPT-maker alleges that tech giant Apple stole trade secrets through a former employee.
articles.preview: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee. In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.
articles.body:
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.

Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.

OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".

The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".

OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.

Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".

A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.

OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

Milioni di testi, immagini, canzoni e video alimentano i modelli d’intelligenza artificiale generativa (ia). I paesi dell’Unione non hanno ancora trovato una linea comune e le pressioni delle aziende, che non vogliono regole troppo stringenti, si fa sentire sia sui parlamenti nazionali sia a livello europeo.

articles.body:
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.

As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

articles.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
articles.summary: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed exec with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair, is a Chinese spy.
articles.preview: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week. What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S.
articles.body:
The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.

The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

- Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.

- If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?

- Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all? The likeliest answer is a leak. A source told CNN that Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence in May, yet Trump has since said he only recently learned of the concerns, and in October he presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. Officials who felt they could not get through to the president may have turned to reporters instead, which would explain how the contents of a memo whose existence has never been disputed found their way into print. What remains unclear is who leaked it, and whether they anticipated the fallout.

There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.

articles.body:
Dalla filiera 96,5 miliardi di fatturato e un contributo del 14,8% al Pil regionale. Le proposte per attrarre gli investimenti in ricerca e valorizzare la prevenzione

Consolidare la posizione della Lombardia per farla diventare l’Hub europeo di riferimento delle Life science oltre a trasformarla in un laboratorio nazionale per l’attrazione dei preziosi investimenti nella ricerca di nuovi farmaci su cui l’Italia perde terreno. E poi farne l’ambasciatrice in Europa della bandiera della prevenzione da trattare come un investimento e non come un costo visto che ogni euro speso in vaccini e screening ne produce come minimo 2,81 di ritorno grazie ai risparmi su malattie e cure evitate. Eccola la road map disegnata da Assolombarda che ieri ha riunito tutti i protagonisti della filiera al Milano Life science forum per aggiornare i suoi numeri da record, ma anche per guardare avanti e provare a difendere questo primato di fronte a una concorrenza sempre più agguerrita che oltre agli Usa vede la Cina correre nella ricerca e nel lancio di nuovi farmaci che per la prima volta hanno superato quelli di Europa e Stati Uniti messi insieme.

I numeri contenuti nel report messo a punto dal Centro studi di Assolombarda insieme al Cergas Bocconi parlano da soli: nel 2025 il fatturato della filiera lombarda che può contare su un ecosistema fatto di imprese (farmaci, biomedicale, biotech, sanità digitale, commercio), ospedali, Irccs, università, centri di ricerca e start up raggiunge i 96,5 miliardi di fatturato con 365mila addetti e soprattutto genera un valore aggiunto di 33,9 miliardi. Una cifra che sale a 76,3 miliardi se si conta il contributo complessivo diretto, indiretto e indotto delle Life Science: in pratica il 14,8% del Pil lombardo. Non solo: la Regione produce ormai il 31,4% del valore della produzione italiana del settore e oltre un quarto del valore aggiunto (26,2%) e rispetto al 2019 il fatturato cresce del 39,6% e il valore aggiunto del 34,8%, numeri superiori alla media nazionale e all’inflazione cumulata.

A trainare la crescita è soprattutto l’industria, che nel 2025 genera 44,5 miliardi di produzione e 12,8 miliardi di valore aggiunto: delle prime 150 imprese industriali italiane del settore per fatturato, 107 (oltre sette su dieci) sono presenti in Lombardia. Infine la Regione si conferma anche un eccellente ecosistema della ricerca con un terzo circa di pubblicazioni e brevetti italiani e con quasi la metà degli studi clinici (il 43%) valutati in Italia che ha coinvolto almeno un centro lombardo. Anche se nel confronto con i poli europei “gemelli”- quello francese (Île-de-France) e tedesco (Baden-Württemberg) - soffre sul numero di brevetti, segno di debolezza sul trasferimento tecnologico, mentre primeggia su pubblicazioni valore aggiunto farmaceutico per abitante e crescita dell’export.

«Sono risultati che testimoniano il grande lavoro che le nostre imprese fanno ogni giorno e che spiegano perché il nostro territorio sia tra i più attrattivi in Europa per gli investimenti in questo settore», sottolinea il presidente di Assolombarda Alvise Biffi. Che però ieri ha invitato tutti a non considerarli una «rendita» perché «gli investimenti in questo settore vanno dove trovano tempi certi e regole che ne riconoscono il valore. Alla politica chiediamo le condizioni per trasformare l’eccellenza lombarda in un vantaggio competitivo stabile per tutto il Paese». Nascono da qui i due paper presentati da Assolombarda al Milano Life science forum: uno che individua una serie di colli di bottiglia nell’attrazione degli investimenti in ricerca clinica (procedure da semplificare, contratti da uniformare e poca trasparenza dei tariffari) che ha visto dopo Germania e Francia anche il sorpasso della Spagna, mentre il secondo paper spinge sulla possibilità di considerare le spese in prevenzione - circa 1,3 miliardi - come un investimento, scomputandole dal calcolo del deficit come è accaduto difesa ed energia. Sul primo fronte l’assessore lombardo al Welfare Guido Bertolaso ieri ha preso l’impegno a creare presto - come chiesto da Assolombarda - una cabina di regìa per superare insieme i colli di bottiglia. Mentre l’idea di considerare anche contabilmente le spese in prevenzione come un investimento ha incassato tantissimi sì da istituzioni, politici e imprenditori con l’impegno a guardare ai prossimi appuntamenti europei come una occasione imperdibile per sostenerla. «Sulla prevenzione - spiega Nicoletta Luppi, vicepresidente di Assolombarda con delega a Life Science & Europa - chiediamo regole che riconoscano ciò che genera valore nel tempo. A livello europeo, il nuovo bilancio pluriennale dell’Unione e la revisione delle regole contabili sono due finestre che l’Italia non può lasciarsi sfuggire, soprattutto visto che ci apprestiamo al semestre di turno per la Presidenza del Consiglio dell’Unione europea. Sulla ricerca clinica la Lombardia è un’eccellenza: ora - conclude Luppi - deve trasformarla in attrattività. Il filo che lega questi temi è uno solo: non guardare alla salute con l’orizzonte di un singolo esercizio di bilancio. Sarà il nostro impegno anche per il 2027, a Milano come a Roma e a Bruxelles».

articles.title: Si rafforzano le intese con la Catalogna
articles.summary: La Regione Lombardia e la Catalogna non solo continueranno a essere alleate per rafforzare la competitività della loro economia e per cogliere nuove opportunità, ma da ieri hanno deciso di...
articles.preview: Dichiarazione congiunta per favorire nuove sinergie e rafforzare il ruolo nella Ue La Regione Lombardia e la Catalogna non solo continueranno a essere alleate per rafforzare la competitività della loro economia e per cogliere nuove opportunità, ma da ieri hanno deciso di rafforzare il loro sodalizio con la firma di una dichiarazione congiunta che porta la firma dell’assessore allo Sviluppo Economico lombardo, Guido Guidesi, e del ministro regionale dell’Impresa e del lavoro della Generalitat de Catalunya Miquel Samper I Rodriguez.
articles.body:
Dichiarazione congiunta per favorire nuove sinergie e rafforzare il ruolo nella Ue

La Regione Lombardia e la Catalogna non solo continueranno a essere alleate per rafforzare la competitività della loro economia e per cogliere nuove opportunità, ma da ieri hanno deciso di rafforzare il loro sodalizio con la firma di una dichiarazione congiunta che porta la firma dell’assessore allo Sviluppo Economico lombardo, Guido Guidesi, e del ministro regionale dell’Impresa e del lavoro della Generalitat de Catalunya Miquel Samper I Rodriguez. Il documento evidenzia la volontà forte di consolidare la collaborazione tra i due territori e di unire le forze rispetto ai rapporti con l’Unione europea. Al centro dell’intesa il rafforzamento della competitività dell’industria europea, il confronto sulle politiche comunitarie, la promozione di iniziative condivise e lo sviluppo di nuove opportunità di sinergie tra imprese, università, centri di ricerca e associazioni dei rispettivi territori.

La collaborazione tra le due regioni esiste da tempo ed è cominciata dal settore della chimica, per proseguire nell’aerospazio, nella produzione di chip e nell’elettronica. «Lombardia e Catalogna sono due territori affini da un punto di vista economico e culturale che condividono una forte identità industriale e una straordinaria capacità imprenditoriale. Siamo due motori economici d’Europa e proprio per questo abbiamo la responsabilità e l’interesse di fare squadra - ha detto Guidesi - mettendo a fattor comune esperienze, competenze e capacità di rappresentanza». Sàmper ha aggiunto che con «la dichiarazione congiunta viene consolidato un rapporto istituzionale ed economico sviluppato attraverso diversi momenti di confronto».

Un passaggio molto importante dell’alleanza tra Lombardia e Catalogna è quello del novembre 2025, quando a Barcellona l’assessore Guidesi e il ministro Sàmper hanno concordato di intensificare le relazioni tra i rispettivi ecosistemi industriali, individuando nella chimica uno degli ambiti prioritari di collaborazione. Il percorso è proseguito nel marzo 2026, con l’incontro a Palazzo Lombardia tra Guidesi e Sàmper che ha avuto come focus l’industria chimica, in particolare la sinergia nell’ambito dell’European Chemical Regions Network (Ecrn), la rete che riunisce le Regioni europee a forte vocazione chimica.

Tra le iniziative condivise nei confronti delle istituzioni comunitarie, i temi prioritari sono il costo dell’energia, la concorrenza internazionale, la transizione ambientale e tecnologica, la sicurezza degli approvvigionamenti e la salvaguardia delle capacità produttive e dell’occupazione. L’obiettivo è favorire connessioni dirette tra le imprese lombarde e catalane, rafforzando le rispettive filiere e valorizzando le opportunità offerte dai programmi e dagli strumenti di finanziamento europei.

articles.preview: Nei primi cinque mesi dall’apertura della piattaforma del GSE (Gestore dei Servizi Energetici) il 12 giugno, sono stati già prenotati in Veneto investimenti per circa 1,3 miliardi di euro (1.264 milioni, per l’esattezza) in beni strumentali per la trasformazione digitale e impianti per l’autoproduzione di energia da fonti rinnovabili, agevolabili con l’iperammortamento.
articles.body:
Nei primi cinque mesi dall’apertura della piattaforma del GSE (Gestore dei Servizi Energetici) il 12 giugno, sono stati già prenotati in Veneto investimenti per circa 1,3 miliardi di euro (1.264 milioni, per l’esattezza) in beni strumentali per la trasformazione digitale e impianti per l’autoproduzione di energia da fonti rinnovabili, agevolabili con l’iperammortamento. Il Veneto è la seconda regione per peso degli investimenti, con il 13,8% sul totale dei 9,18 miliardi prenotati a livello nazionale, dietro a Lombardia (2,16 miliardi) e davanti ad Emilia-Romagna (925 milioni), Piemonte (790 milioni), Campania (536) e Trentino-Alto Adige (513). Fra le province, Brescia (5,7%) precede Milano (4,7%), Bergamo, Bolzano, Treviso, Vicenza.

Sono i dati resi disponibili dal Ministero delle Imprese e del Made in Italy (Mimit), aggiornati al 19 novembre: il nuovo iperammortamento ha raccolto 32.324 comunicazioni valide, presentate da 21.851 imprese, per un valore complessivo di 9,18 miliardi di euro di investimenti comunicati in poco più di cinque mesi, tre quarti già confermati con il versamento dell’acconto (20%), prossimi a raggiungere il valore di 10 miliardi. Il 98% degli investimenti riguarda i beni materiali, l’1,3% i software, sui quali pesa l’esclusione dei servizi in abbonamento (as a service), e lo 0,7% impianti da fonti rinnovabili. Le piccole imprese rappresentano il 60% delle comunicazioni e il 32% del valore (151mila euro in media), le grandi imprese il 17% delle comunicazioni e il 40% del valore (657mila euro l’investimento mediano). In un caso su tre si tratta di un acquisto in leasing. Il 66% degli investimenti è concentrato al Nord, il 16% al Centro, il 18% nel Mezzogiorno.

«In un quadro così complesso - commenta Paola Carron, Presidente di Confindustria Veneto Est - il dato sulle richieste dell’iperammortamento per investimenti 5.0, quasi raddoppiate da agosto, testimonia la risposta vigorosa da parte delle imprese del Veneto a questo strumento, che sta dando sicuramente un impulso agli investimenti in nuove tecnologie, oggi più che mai cruciali per rimanere competitivi».

«Diamo atto al Mimit di avere migliorato il nuovo piano, dopo le criticità e incertezze del credito d’imposta e degli “esodati” 5.0, e messo in campo una misura con durata pluriennale. Questo per la manifattura è decisamente importante. L’obiettivo è avere misure semplici, stabili nel tempo: non cambiamo quelle che funzionano. Al contempo, auspichiamo che il confronto parlamentare sulla Manovra veda il massimo sforzo per rafforzare il sostegno agli investimenti e alla crescita, con un sistema di incentivi più ampio, stabile e adeguatamente finanziato, un’estensione dell’iperammortamento fino al termine del 2029, e un incentivo concreto per i canoni dei software con abbonamento. Oggi è la modalità prevalente con cui le imprese adottano software e servizi digitali. Riconoscere anche gli investimenti in formazione e beni immateriali, è la via per favorire l’acquisizione di competenze e nuove tecnologie, come l’intelligenza artificiale, soprattutto nelle PMI, essenziali per aumentare produttività e competitività. Ora bisogna lavorare insieme per utilizzare al meglio questa leva e supportare il dinamismo e le aspettative del sistema produttivo», conclude Paola Carron.
